node.label: Eric Williams
node.description: Argues that slavery and slave-trade wealth contributed to British capitalist development, and that changing economic interests helped explain abolition. These are related but distinguishable theses whose mechanisms, timing, and weight remain debated. His work challenges accounts centered on European benevolence.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Distinguish the original book from later editions and from subsequent arguments about capitalism and slavery.
node.scope_note: The 1944 preface separates slavery’s contribution to industrial finance from industrial capitalism’s role in abolition; the conclusion gives economic forces explanatory priority. Williams names Ragatz, Pitman, Herskovits, Burch and Harlow among scholarly helpers. Drescher’s 1977 challenge concerns decline and the 1807 slave-trade abolition, not a refutation of every slavery/capitalism claim. From Columbus to Castro (1970) is a later Caribbean synthesis, here checked only bibliographically.

incident_edges.relationship: challenges benevolent accounts of empire and abolition
incident_edges.evidence_note: Represents a contested historical argument rather than an established explanation of every abolition process. Capitalism and Slavery challenges explanations centred on imperial benevolence; the debate about its economic claims remains open.

incident_edges.relationship: makes slavery’s relationship to capitalist development a central historical problem
incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1944 preface states two economic questions. The recorded Drescher criticism addresses decline and abolition; it does not automatically resolve industrial financing, later regional histories or other abolition processes.

incident_edges.relationship: informs Rodney’s intellectual formation through Capitalism and Slavery
incident_edges.evidence_note: Michael West’s 2018 assessment reproduced by Verso names Capitalism and Slavery as formative. This remains a secondary attribution: no direct Rodney passage was located in this batch, and the two historical explanations are not identical.

incident_edges.relationship: Williams links British development with slave and colonial trades
incident_edges.evidence_note: The primary 1944 preface states a transregional economic question. Neither this framing nor the later 1970 synthesis proves every causal mechanism or establishes membership in later Atlantic historiography.

incident_edges.relationship: Drescher contests the economic-decline explanation for 1807 abolition (1977, in the publisher's description of Econocide); Eltis and Engerman judge the growth linkages of slavery to British industry small (2000, as Hilt reports)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In its publisher's description (the monograph is unread), Econocide (1977) emphasizes continued economic potential and public mobilization. This is one named intervention within economic/abolition debates, not the entire field’s verdict or a test of all Williams’s propositions. Full statistical evidence remains unchecked. The arrow concerns the decline-and-abolition and growth-linkage questions; slave-derived wealth in British society is carried by Hall's edges. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates and added further named readers. Drescher's own retrospect ('Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years', 1997, opening read) names 'the Williams-Drescher debate' and calls the book 'a classic' that reoriented the subject. Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000, unread; mediated) concluded, as Hilt reports (JEH 2017, p. 516), that 'the total value added and growth-inducing linkages of the British slave trade and Caribbean slave plantations were not particularly large'; Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 226) quote Solow's middle position, that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (1987, p. 72), and judge that Williams's 'contemporary defenders … use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227).
incident_edges.map_label: Decline and abolition disputed; slavery’s weight questioned, 1977–2000

incident_edges.relationship: Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery tested on the compensation records: supported on slave-wealth in British society, qualified on decline, and set against a British Marxist pantheon that left James and Williams out (2009–2014)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014). "C. L. R James and Eric Williams did not appear in their pantheon. James and Williams, in their struggle against racism and colonialism insisted on the linkage between metropole and colony … the intimate connections … between capitalism and slavery" (p. 23). "Williams never argued that slavery 'caused' the Industrial Revolution … as Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland and I suggest in the co-authored book which documents the results of the first phase of our project on the Legacies of British Slave-Ownership (LBS), there is a move to a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians" (p. 24); "Williams’s insight into the importance of slave-derived wealth to eighteenth-century society and culture has been greatly expanded" (p. 24). Qualifications: the modified thesis is attributed jointly to the LBS authors and set among economic historians (Pomeranz, Inikori); it is not a claim that slavery caused industrialization. The jointly written introduction to Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014; read in part by the second research pass, without print pages) tests Williams directly: "Eric Williams' Capitalism and Slavery included four connected arguments that are critical for us"; "our findings are entirely supportive of Williams in the context of this second thesis" (slave-wealth in British society); on industrialisation "Our material cannot resolve these controversies"; and the work "complicates Williams by qualifying his 'decline' thesis". Katie Donington, a co-author, recalls that "The project foregrounded Williams's work" (Black Perspectives, 2020). Hall was the project's principal investigator (REF 2014 case study).

incident_edges.relationship: Capitalism and Slavery (1944) as the starting point of the slavery-and-capitalism component: four arguments taken up and modified by economic historians and by the new history of capitalism
incident_edges.evidence_note: Readers, read: Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 227): 'Four of his arguments are critical to the NHC project: that slavery was central to the Industrial Revolution; that slave wealth was important to the history of eighteenth-century Britain; that the West Indian slave economy went into decline from 1783; and that West Indian slave-owners moved from being a progressive force within mercantilism to being a reactionary force within industrial capitalism'; 'His contemporary defenders, however, use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227); 'a movement among economic historians that accepts a modified version of the Williams thesis' (p. 233). Hilt (JEH 2017, p. 516): 'Like Eric Williams in Capitalism and Slavery (1944), Beckert argues …'; n. 6: Inikori (2002) is 'the strongest recent defense of the Williams hypothesis'. Regele (2023, p. 7): the new work draws on 'a long history of scholarship … most notably Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery'. Pomeranz (2000, p. 3 n. 2): 'the generally negative current mainstream verdicts on the arguments of Eric Williams (1944)'. Distinct from edge_155 (Williams → economic) and edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

incident_edges.relationship: Davis disputes Williams’s economic-decline explanation of British abolition while explicitly separating it from slavery’s contribution to industrialization.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2012 reply to Barbara Solow, whose contrary evidence and defense remain explicit in the exchange. Davis limits his repudiation to the decline/abolition hypothesis and credits Williams for initiating the debate; his strong consensus language is his assessment, not the atlas’s final verdict. Williams1944, Ryden and the cited economic histories remain unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: James, Williams and Césaire challenge different imperial historical narratives
named_group_routes.evidence_note: James, Williams, and Rodney challenge different imperial narratives; national liberation is not a single explanatory position. Césaire’s checked opening attacks civilizing claims; Williams’s economic propositions remain disputed.

named_group_routes.relationship: extends analysis to unequal international relations
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Williams and Rodney make empire, slavery, and unequal development historical problems. This does not derive all dependency theory from a generic field. Frank’s notes add particular Latin American histories, including Furtado and Góngora, used selectively rather than as a generic economics origin.

named_group_routes.relationship: Comparative development and the resources of empire: economic-history questions taken into global history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Comparative development and transregional exchange are resources, not a claim that all global history adopts economic modelling. Williams's argument on slavery and capitalism and the comparison of Eurasian economies are among the economic-history questions global history takes up. Pomeranz's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.130). Huang’s 2002 criticism and Pomeranz’s reply document a later disagreement over the 2000 comparison; neither is a settled verdict or an extension of mapped coverage.

named_group_routes.relationship: James’s changing historical and dramatic work recasts Marxist questions through enslaved revolution
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The earlier wording grouped James and Williams too closely under Marxist social history. Individual entries now distinguish their arguments. James is a specified participant who recasts Marxist historical questions through slavery and revolution. Not all anti-colonial thinkers share that position. Douglas’s publisher description supplies edition-specific support, not a single Marxist identity for the umbrella.

named_group_routes.relationship: Rodney and Williams connect empire with distinct explanations of unequal economic change
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Rodney and Williams provide distinct arguments concerning empire and economic change; neither stands for every dependency theorist. Rodney’s primary excerpt emphasizes power and control; its broad loss-of-agency rhetoric remains his argument.

named_group_routes.relationship: Hall uses hegemony and common sense to relate cultural struggle and social organization
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Primary pp. 62 and 69 discuss Williams’s Gramscian turn and Hall’s use of common sense/organization to address theoretical tensions. This strengthens a specific reception claim; it does not make Gramsci the field’s sole origin.

named_group_routes.relationship: Thompson’s cultural class history enters the field and its internal disagreements
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Hall’s primary pp. 58 and 62–63 identify The Making as a seminal work and discuss Thompson’s 1961 criticism of Williams. Class history already has cultural questions; later theoretical criticism is not discovery of culture in a previously noncultural field.

named_group_routes.relationship: Cultural studies and cultural history share questions about meanings and everyday practices
named_group_routes.evidence_note: An editorial comparison of distinct research practices. Literary criticism, ethnography and semiotic readings should not be collapsed into one historical method; the supplied sources do not establish a general transmission to every cultural historian. A particular resource is now documented: Spiegel cites Raymond Williams on cultural production through Alan Sinfield’s typescript. This mediated citation does not turn the broad undirected comparison into a field-wide transmission claim.

named_group_routes.relationship: William Appleman Williams joins ideology and political economy in an interpretation of American expansion
named_group_routes.evidence_note: William Appleman Williams and related historians, not Eric Williams; work-specific reception evidence remains to be added. Norton’s description now supports this named work, while full-text and wider reception remain unchecked. Retain distinction from Eric Williams.

named_group_routes.relationship: James and Williams examine slavery and revolution across imperial boundaries
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Earlier transregional scholarship is not retrospectively assigned a single later Atlantic-school identity. Gilroy’s preface acknowledges limited treatment of James and Fanon; it cannot substantiate detailed reception of either. The separately recorded James/Williams contributions retain their own evidence.

named_group_routes.relationship: provides materialist resources reworked in histories of slavery and revolution
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Retargeted from the anti-colonial umbrella to James. The feedback’s blanket assertion that both James and Eric Williams write as Marxists is not adopted; their distinct arguments remain visible. James’s 1971 recollection names his reading of Trotsky, Lenin and Marx. It supports a specific resource while leaving exact retrospective chronology open; Williams is not assigned the same theoretical identity.

named_group_routes.relationship: Hall identifies Thompson’s cultural class history as a seminal contribution
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Hall’s primary pp. 58 and 62–63 explicitly place The Making in the early cultural reorientation and discuss Thompson’s criticism of Williams. This individual contribution complements the broader Marxist-social-history relationship. It does not identify the American New Left node with the British political context.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black Montreal in the long 1960s
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Austin's Fear of a Black Nation (description read) centres the 1968 Congress of Black Writers and the Black-led protest at Sir George Williams University; Forsythe's 1971 collection is a contemporary participants' account, not scholarship; Austin 2007 is title-level. All selected scholarship is post-2000, so this comparison rests on later work; Canada’s 1960s declined a black – Canada’s 1960s edge for the same reason, and this edge is the narrower Canadian pair. PhD context: 40% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canada’s 1960s (lift 2.8).

named_group_routes.relationship: Coal and New World resources enabled divergence between comparably developed Eurasian cores (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: the critiques now have their own arrows (philip_huang → kenneth_pomeranz; economic → kenneth_pomeranz, which revision 1.145 moved to capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz, with Brenner and Isett drawn separately as robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz). Pomeranz restated the timing in 2003: "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence" (JAS 62:1, p. 179, read). Catherine Hall reads the coal-and-colonies argument as part of "a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians": "Pomeranz sees the Atlantic slave-economy and the availability of coal as the two complementary factors allowing Britain to expand" (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, p. 24, read).

named_group_routes.relationship: Thompson's history of class and culture as a model for Palmer's labour history and the subject of his studies of Thompson (1976–94), with disagreements Palmer stated, including on base and superstructure
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Palmer's 1976 essay (read) cites Thompson's Making for the skilled mechanic's leading role (p. 14 and notes). Bercuson (1981, p. 97, re-read): 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes."' Kealey (1981, p. 82; existing note, not re-read) cites Palmer's forthcoming book as the place where Thompson's work is analysed at length. Palmer's 1987 ILWCH response (notes as listed by the publisher) leans on Thompson: n. 8 cites The Making (pp. 529–40) for how historians have interrogated the language of sources, n. 10 says 'This unity of the political and the economic is fundamental to Thompson's Making', and n. 14 cites The Poverty of Theory (pp. 235–36). 'Homage to Edward Thompson', Labour/Le Travail 32 (1993) and 33 (1994), read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18: Palmer sets out Thompson's socialist humanism against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor' (Part I, p. 68) and quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (Part II, p. 17; Thompson's interviews, cited in n. 9, not read). Palmer's two books on Thompson, The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981) and E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994), are cited at title and imprint level only (Open Library). Stated disagreement, in period: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) notes that Descent into Discourse 'takes Thompson and Raymond Williams to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure' (pp. 209–11 of the book, unread here). Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer's 1993 interview in Left History: 'it was relooking at The Making that convinced me to do labour history' (Left History 1:2, 1993, pp. 111–12, as quoted; the journal's PDF was behind a bot wall); Rogers calls The Making 'an exemplary model' for Palmer's dissertation, finds Palmer 'sympathetic and defensive of Thompson's position', but notes that 'Palmer does not necessarily agree with Thompson's reading of Marx' and 'is not a wholehearted advocate of Thompson's socialist humanism', since he holds to a revolutionary vanguard. Influence, not discipleship: the arrow records Thompson's work as Palmer's model and subject; it does not claim that Palmer adopted Thompson's positions whole.

named_group_routes.relationship: From within Marxism, rejects the 'economic automatism' of Stalinist base-and-superstructure Marxism and the treatment of class as 'a thing', holding to the 'dialectical interaction between social consciousness ... and social being' and faulting Marx's own 'clumsy static model' (1957–78)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Thompson's own in-period statements. (1) 'Socialist Humanism: An Epistle to the Philistines', The New Reasoner 1 (Summer 1957), pp. 105–143, read in full in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription (no page numbers). Of Stalinist theory: 'How much easier if the people had no minds, if the "superstructure" was cut out and society was all "base"'; 'This economic automatism certainly is not Marxism.' 'In all their historical analysis Marx and Engels always kept in view this dialectical interaction between social consciousness (both active and passive) and social being. But in trying to explain their ideas they expressed them as a make-belief "model", the "basis" of social relations (in production) and the "superstructure" ... In fact no such basis and superstructure ever existed; it is a metaphor to help us to understand what does exist – men, who act, experience, think and act again. It turns out that it is a bad and dangerous model, since Stalin used it not as an image of men changing in society but as a mechanical model, operating semi-automatically and independently of conscious human agency.' 'An idea is not a reflex of a gasometer'; 'No "basis" ever invented a steam engine, or sat on the National Coal Board.' He does not exempt Marx: 'because Marx reduced his concept of process to a clumsy static model, Stalinism evolved this mystique'; features of Stalinism 'can be traced to ambiguities in the thought of Marx and, even more, to mechanistic fallacies in Lenin's writings'. Stalinism's three features are 'anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'. The revolt against Stalinism 'will, if successful, confirm the revolutionary confidence of the founders of the socialist movement'. (2) Preface to The Making of the English Working Class (1963), university-hosted transcription read in full (transcription pp. 1–2; printed pagination not collated): class is 'something which in fact happens (and can be shown to have happened) in human relationships'; 'There is today an ever-present temptation to suppose that class is a thing. This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing', in which the class-consciousness that '"it" ought to have' is deduced and 'a cultural superstructure' lets recognition dawn 'in inefficient ways'; 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.' The same passage finds 'a similar error ... on the other side of the ideological divide', in the static sociology of Smelser and Dahrendorf, so the preface's target is reification in both camps. The preface's 'I am seeking to rescue the poor stockinger ...' is aimed at Fabian, economic-historian and 'Pilgrim's Progress' orthodoxies, not at Marxism, and is not used here. (3) 'The Poverty of Theory' (1978), section x, re-read in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription: 'Stalinism afforded a caricature of Marxism, which offered ... an identical reification of process, in which a "superstructure" was reduced to confirming or legitimating a base' (the identity is with Smelser's sociology), and no analogies 'derived from mechanical or organic mechanism' can 'encompass the logic of indeterminate historical process', since no analogy from another area can have 'any more than a limited, illustrative, metaphoric value (and often, as with basis and superstructure, a static and damaging one)'; in section vii he calls himself 'deeply indebted for certain concepts to Marx's own practice'. In-period readings: Palmer's 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993, Part I, p. 68) describes Thompson's socialist humanism as directed against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor', and (1994, Part II, p. 17) quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (from interviews, not read). The critique was itself contested inside Marxism: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) reports that Palmer's Descent into Discourse took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. Later reading, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) sees in Thompson a 'rejection of economic determinism and the base–superstructure model of explanation favoured by many Marxists', preferring 'the co-determination of social being and social consciousness, mediated by experience'. Scope: a critique of economistic and Stalinist uses of historical materialism, and of Marx's own static model, made from within Marxism; it is not a rejection of historical materialism. The Althusser critique stays on edge_310 (ep_thompson → althusser) and edge_027 (marx → althusser); his contribution to Marxist social history stays on edge_309 (ep_thompson → marx).

named_group_routes.relationship: Popper, Lakatos and the historian L. Pearce Williams criticise Kuhn's normal science and theory change: indoctrination, irrationalism, "mob psychology" and too little history (1965–70), answered by Kuhn
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period texts read in Lakatos and Musgrave, eds., Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge (1970; the 1965 Bedford College symposium). Popper, already a critic on the science roster: the normal scientist "has been taught in a dogmatic spirit: he is a victim of indoctrination" (p. 53); "Kuhn's logic is the logic of historical relativism" (p. 55); the Myth of the Framework "is, in our time, the central bulwark of irrationalism" (p. 56); yet "'Normal' science, in Kuhn's sense, exists" (p. 52). Lakatos, a contributor on the science roster: Kuhn's message "had some authoritarian and irrationalist overtones" (p. 92 n. 3); "in Kuhn's view scientific revolution is irrational, a matter for mob psychology" (p. 178, italicised in the original); he also absorbs Kuhn, offering his research programmes as a reconstruction of Kuhn's "socio-psychological concept of 'paradigm'" (p. 179 n. 1). L. Pearce Williams, a historian of science, aims at Kuhn and Popper alike: "the history of science cannot bear such a load at this time. We simply do not know enough to permit a philosophical structure to be erected on a historical foundation"; "As a historian, then, I must view both Popper and Kuhn with a somewhat jaundiced eye" (p. 50), while continuing to use both as guides. Kuhn's replies: charges of "irrationality, relativism, and the defence of mob rule" are "labels which I categorically reject" (p. 234); such misinterpretations "are voiced only by philosophers" (p. 260); to Pearce Williams, "There is no area in which I am more deeply conscious of the need for additional historical research, though I dissent from the conclusions Pearce Williams draws from that need" (pp. 251–252); and in the 1970 Postscript, good reasons "function as values" (p. 199) and "That is not a relativist's position" (p. 206). The irrationalism charge came from philosophers on the science roster; the historian's objection was evidential. edge_332 (science → kuhn, influence) stays.

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault's notion of discourse used to identify Orientalism, with an explicit disagreement over the weight of individual authors (1978)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked): 'I have found it useful here to employ Michel Foucault's notion of a discourse, as described by him in The Archaeology of Knowledge and in Discipline and Punish, to identify Orientalism. My contention is that without examining Orientalism as a discourse one cannot possibly understand the enormously systematic discipline by which European culture was able to manage—and even produce—the Orient politically, sociologically, militarily, ideologically, scientifically, and imaginatively during the post-Enlightenment period' (p. 3). 'Yet unlike Michel Foucault, to whose work I am greatly indebted, I do believe in the determining imprint of individual writers upon the otherwise anonymous collective body of texts constituting a discursive formation like Orientalism'; 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23). Elsewhere he writes of 'what Michel Foucault calls a discourse, whose material presence or weight, not the originality of a given author, is really responsible for the texts produced out of it' (p. 94), and he groups 'Gramsci, certainly, and Foucault and Raymond Williams in their very different ways' as illustrating that hegemonic culture's constraints on writers 'were productive, not unilaterally inhibiting' (p. 14). In-period criticism of the combination: al-'Azm (1981, read) objects that for Said 'representations, images, words, metaphors ... are, if not the very stuff of reality, then certainly much more important and informative substitutes for raw reality itself'. Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 289–290) sets the p. 23 and p. 94 passages against each other and argues that 'Foucault and Gramsci have different and contrasting notions of discourse'; Ahmad (1991–92) is reported by Irwin (p. 300) as finding that 'Said's allegiance to Foucault ... got him into the worst muddles'; Ahmad's texts were not read. The edge records Said's stated use and revision of Foucault, not a reading of Foucault's own position; Said's later criticism is edge 4.

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault criticised for discounting individual authors (1978) and for ignoring empire and dissolving the individual in a 'microphysics of power' that it is 'hopeless to resist' (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (1978): 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23), while declaring himself 'greatly indebted' to Foucault (p. 23). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): of Foucault and Raymond Williams, 'In the main I am in considerable sympathy with the genealogical discoveries of these two formidable scholars, and greatly indebted to them. Yet for both the imperial experience is quite irrelevant, a theoretical oversight that is the norm in Western cultural and scientific disciplines' (p. 41). Comparing Foucault and Fanon: 'Foucault's work moves further and further away from serious consideration of social wholes, focussing instead upon the individual as dissolved in an ineluctably advancing "microphysics of power" that it is hopeless to resist'; 'ignoring the imperial context of his own theories, Foucault seems actually to represent an irresistible colonizing movement that paradoxically fortifies the prestige of both the lonely individual scholar and the system that contains him'; Foucault 'swerves away from politics entirely' (p. 278). His note 198 refers the reader to 'my critique in "Foucault and the Imagination of Power"' (in David Hoy, ed., Foucault: A Critical Reader, 1986, pp. 149–155); that essay, and 'Traveling Theory' (1983), were not read. On p. 26 he also describes Foucault's turn to 'the local micro-physics of power that surround the individual'. Foucault's position is given only as Said presents it; no reply by Foucault was looked for. The critique is from a writer who kept using Foucault (edge 2); it is a disagreement within an acknowledged debt. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) records other postcolonial critics' engagements and stays.

named_group_routes.relationship: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’: the two senses of representation, the epistemic violence of colonial law and knowledge, and the subaltern woman silenced between colonial and indigenous patriarchal discourse on sati (1985–99)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay. Later reception, added in revision 1.151: Interventions 4:2 (2002) devoted a special issue to A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, from a panel at the IAPL conference in 2000, with her response (metadata and abstracts only); Mark Sanders's abstract holds that placing "Can the subaltern speak?" in the book's "History" chapter "emphasizes its deconstruction of Marxist politics". Ritu Birla's abstract (the essay is unread) explores "the challenges of radical history writing" through the book's chapter on history, under the themes of "limits, the open secret, and value/transvaluation"; it sets Spivak beside Joan Scott's critique of "experience", opening "a discussion of the supplementary relationship of literature and history", and connects the limit of history to "the selective production of the archive".

named_group_routes.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88); the subaltern later reformulated as those 'removed from lines of social mobility' (2004)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79; this disagreement with Guha is drawn as its own person-to-person critique, Spivak → Guha, in this revision, and is no longer named in this edge's relationship); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. But the theoretically inclined metropolitan identitarians did’ (p. 332). Later reading, labelled: Partha Chatterjee (2010; Morris volume, unpaginated) recalls first reading both essays in 1985 with ‘bewilderment’ and calls her intervention ‘the poststructuralist moment in Subaltern Studies’, adding that a changed political context also drove the shift. A critique from within, not a rejection: she joined the editorial collective in the 1990s. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) carries the same story under the gender entry; see the proposed relabel. Guha’s person edge (pe137_guha_rel_01, guha draft) cites the same 1985 essay as reception; this edge is hers. Later reformulation and reading, added in revision 1.151 and dated after 2000: in "Righting Wrongs" (South Atlantic Quarterly, 2004; read in part, from a February 2001 lecture) she writes, "By subaltern I mean those removed from lines of social mobility" (p. 531), and warns that leaders from the domestic "below" ignore "the historically established discontinuity between themselves and the subaltern" (p. 535). Richard M. Eaton (Journal of World History, 2000, read p. 60) summarises the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians" for "positivist methodologies" (see the truthdebate critique).
named_group_routes.map_label: Strategic essentialism and the gendered subaltern, 1985–2004

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault's account of power criticised as blind to imperialism and the international division of labour, and for an intellectual who lets the oppressed 'speak for themselves' while remaining transparent; his analyses of disciplinary institutions kept as useful (1988)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period text: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint, read in full). She takes as her object ‘Intellectuals and power: a conversation between Michel Foucault and Gilles Deleuze’ (p. 66), whose participants ‘systematically ignore the question of ideology and their own implication in intellectual and economic history’ (p. 66). In her summary of the conversation, ‘the oppressed can know and speak for themselves’ (p. 74); she adds ‘to Said’s analysis the notion of the surreptitious subject of power and desire marked by the transparency of the intellectual’ (p. 75). ‘Foucault is a brilliant thinker of power-in-spacing, but the awareness of the topographical reinscription of imperialism does not inform his presuppositions’ (p. 85); ‘The clinic, the asylum, the prison, the university - all seem to be screen-allegories that foreclose a reading of the broader narratives of imperialism’ (p. 86). She keeps part of his work: ‘what remains useful in Foucault is the mechanics of disciplinarization and institutionalization, the constitution, as it were, of the colonizer’ (p. 90), and calls his model of localized resistance ‘an admirable program’ that, universalized, ‘accommodates unacknowledged privileging of the subject’ (p. 85). Foucault’s position is given only as she presents it, from the translated conversation and Power/Knowledge; no reply was looked for (he died in 1984). Reception: Eagleton (1999, read) groups Derrida and Foucault as thinkers who ‘veer between a cult of theoretical “madness” ... and a more restrained, reformist sort of politics’, a criticism of her allies, not a defence of Foucault. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) carries her name with Stoler’s; see the optional relabel. Said’s separate critique of Foucault is pe137_said_rel_04 (said draft); she cites Said’s criticism and extends it (p. 75).

named_group_routes.relationship: Derrida's deconstruction, which she translated and introduced (1976), used and tested as a method for reading colonial texts and subaltern historiography, without being celebrated 'as feminism as such' (1976–88)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period texts. Translator’s preface to Of Grammatology (1976; read at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition): ‘To locate the promising marginal text, to disclose the undecidable moment, to pry it loose with the positive lever of the signifier; to reverse the resident hierarchy, only to displace it; to dismantle in order to reconstitute what is always already inscribed. Deconstruction in a nutshell. But take away the assurance of the text’s authority, the critic’s control, and the primacy of meaning, and the possession of this formula does not guarantee much.’ Subaltern Studies IV (1985): ‘This is the greatest gift of deconstruction: to question the authority of the investigating subject without paralysing him, persistently transforming conditions of impossibility into possibility’ (p. 336). ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (1985) sets ‘the lessons of deconstruction’ aside for the essay, choosing to ‘strategically take shelter in an essentialism’ (p. 244). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): ‘Derrida is hard to read; his real object of investigation is classical philosophy. Yet he is less dangerous when understood than the first-world intellectual masquerading as the absent nonrepresenter who lets the oppressed speak for themselves’ (p. 87); reading ‘Of grammatology as a positive science’, she reads him as placing the ethnocentric constitution of the Other as ‘Not a general problem, but a European problem’, and ‘As a postcolonial intellectual, I am not troubled that he does not lead me ... to the specific path that such a critique makes necessary’ (p. 89); ‘I have attempted to use and go beyond Derridean deconstruction, which I do not celebrate as feminism as such’ (p. 104); ‘In a certain way, then, the critique of imperialism is deconstruction as such’ (n. 47, p. 108). In-period reception: Eagleton (1999, read) calls Derrida ‘a consecrated figure for this book, about whom hardly a breath of criticism seems permissible’. Prakash (1992; reprint pp. 224–225, read) quotes her definition of deconstruction as an ‘impossible “no” to a structure, which one critiques, yet inhabits intimately’. Later reading, labelled: Chatterjee (2010) recalls that in 1982 the subalternists ‘did not imagine that Jacques Derrida ... could have anything remotely to do with Indian peasants’. Wikidata’s ‘influenced by’ (P737) lists Paul de Man, not Derrida; that is a Wikidata statement, not evidence here. Her translation’s publication dates (first American edition 1976, corrected 1997) are already checked on derrida_grammatology_corrected. edge_025 (derrida → post) tells her story under the group entry; see the proposed relabel.

named_group_routes.relationship: Chakrabarty uses 'Spivak's subaltern' as an analogy for the subject whom university history's transition narrative can only represent, the 'Indian' history that 'cannot speak itself as “theory”' (1992)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Chakrabarty’s in-period text. ‘Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History’, Representations 37 (1992), read (JSTOR copy; spacing restored): the antihistorical subject ‘cannot speak itself as “theory” within the knowledge procedures of the university even when these knowledge procedures acknowledge and “document” its existence. Much like Spivak’s “subaltern” (or the anthropologist’s peasant who can only have a quoted existence in a larger statement that belongs to the anthropologist alone), this subject can only be spoken for and spoken of by the transition narrative’ (p. 19, n. 52, citing ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ and her 1990 Socialist Review interview). He also borrows, ‘in Gayatri Spivak’s words’, ‘the feeling of community that belongs to national links and political organizations’ (p. 18, n. 48, citing the 1988 essay at p. 277; Williams and Chrisman reprint p. 72); she is among those thanked in the unnumbered first note (p. 23), and n. 43 (p. 25) credits her with an expression (‘personal communication’). Her side, in period: Subaltern Studies IV (1985) discusses his labour essays (pp. 331, 344) and sets them against the collective’s neglect of gender: ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357). The influence is bounded: Chakrabarty’s provincializing argument ‘follows directly’ from his work in Subaltern Studies (2000, p. 15; on edge_914), and the guha draft proposes Guha → Chakrabarty for the critique of the ‘pre-political’. This edge records one acknowledged borrowing in the 1992 programmatic essay, not a genealogy.
named_group_routes.map_label: ‘Spivak’s subaltern’ in the artifice of history, 1992

named_group_routes.relationship: Workers' control and class at the centre: Toronto skilled workers' power on the job (1976) and their responses to industrial capitalism (1980), with a periodization by stages of capitalism and a case for class analysis and the materiality of culture (1978–81); contested by Bercuson and Brody (1981) and by feminist critics (1987–2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. '“The Honest Workingman” and Workers’ Control', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 32–68, read at pp. 32–34 and 58–62: 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized. … In Toronto work places, craftsmen employed their monopoly on skill and experience to dictate terms to their employers … which, in modern parlance, gave to these late nineteenth century craftsmen a high degree of workers' control of production' (p. 32); he draws on David Montgomery's 'veterans of industrial life' and on Raymond Williams's 'residual' and 'emergent' (p. 33); 'The custom of workers' control, widely regarded as a right, had become deeply embedded in working class culture' and its defence 'became the major locus of class struggle in the opening decades of the twentieth century' (p. 62). 'The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing', Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), pp. 116–135, read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: historians still treat the new study of class 'as little more than interesting additional facts', but 'the new history is well on its way to transforming our understanding of the entire course and structure of Canadian development' (p. 116). 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 67–94, read in full: the project 'never excluded the study of unions and labour politics', nor called for history 'simply "written from the bottom up," since it always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); a periodization of 'pre-industrial capitalism to 1850; industrial capitalism, 1850 to the mid-1890s; monopoly capitalism, 1890s to 1929; and crisis and reconstruction, 1930 to the present', offered as 'at best tentative' (p. 74); 'I will certainly stand with scholars such as Thompson and Williams who have argued persuasively for the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); class 'does have an "objective" side', but '"Class-for-itself," or the failure of the working class to develop such, is almost by definition what working-class history concerns itself with' (pp. 85–86); work on the 1880s found 'a class surprisingly united', in which divisions 'of ethnicity, skill, religion, and even sex were recognized, debated, and for a few years in the 1880s, at least, were overcome', and 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89). He places himself among scholars who were 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93). Toronto Workers (1980) is unread; Brody quotes its introduction: 'The work will have succeeded to the extent that it provides convincing evidence that the working class was not just "made" but rather was the result of a dialectical interplay of class forces in which it was one of the actors' (p. xviii, as quoted). In-period critics. David Bercuson, in the same issue (pp. 95–96, read), quotes the 1976 Essays definition of the new labour history and notes that 'Kealey's study of Toronto workers contains at least five chapters devoted to working-class and trade-union politics'; his wider objections are recorded under wcreq_bercuson_1981 and edge_919. David Brody, review, Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), pp. 361–364, read in full: 'Kealey thus lays the foundation, hitherto largely lacking, for a history of the Toronto labour movement' (p. 362), but 'It is in the interpretation of this information that the book founders'; 'Every strike signifies "class conflict," every labour involvement in public life "class politics"' (p. 363); 'Having overreached himself, he has produced only a useable one' (p. 364). Ian McKay, 'Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), cites Kealey's 1981 'defence of the term' (p. 214 n. 88) and argues that working-class culture has 'weak explanatory value' and that Williams's residual and emergent categories 'merely have allowed social historians to indulge in retrospective cheerleading for progressive ideas' (p. 223 and n. 122); Kealey in 1981 called McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.). Bettina Bradbury (1987, pp. 35–36, read) and Joan Sangster (2000, p. 133, read): see edge pe138_kealey_rel_05 and the node; Sangster: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (p. 133, of Kealey and Warrian's Essays, 1976). Desmond Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; 'If, as Kealey insisted, Toronto's working class achieved unity across ethnic and sectarian barriers, it must have been for the briefest of moments in the city contemporaries sometimes called "the Belfast of North America"'. A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names him in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; he presents the work as 'conceived collectively' (1981, p. 68 n. 8). Scope: this edge is Kealey's own contribution; edge_919 carries Palmer's craft culture, edge_886 and edge_890 the Marxist and Thompsonian resources. The Knights of Labor book (1982) is unread and appears in pe138_kealey_rel_05.

named_group_routes.relationship: Herbert Gutman's cultural history of American workers and David Montgomery's workers' control as models for Kealey's Toronto studies (1976–81), as Kealey and his reviewers said, with the criticisms of Gutman he reported and Brody's verdict that he did not follow Gutman's method
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statements. 1976 (Labour/Le Travailleur 1, read at pp. 32–34, 58): 'David Montgomery has suggested that we must look beyond pre-industrial cultural forms if we are to understand the behaviour of skilled workers', who were 'veterans of industrial life' (p. 33); on the meaning of shop-floor power, 'David Montgomery has argued that the major impact of this early workers' control was the skilled workers' growing awareness that the key institution for the transformation of society was the trade union' (p. 58). 1978 (Acadiensis, p. 117): the works of Thompson and Hobsbawm, 'and later of Americans such as Herbert Gutman and David Montgomery, had their effects in Canada on a new generation of graduate students'. 1981 (Labour/Le Travailleur 7, read in full): 'A cultural approach in American work on labour history also generated a significant breakthrough. Most notably associated with Herbert Gutman' (p. 81); n. 33: 'Gutman's influence can be seen in numerous recent studies. In Canada see Palmer, A Culture in Conflict and Kealey, Toronto Workers' (p. 82). He reports Dubofsky's and Montgomery's worry about 'the failure to consider the political and economic context' and Brody's charge that Gutman 'shifted the Thompsonian focus on class and culture into a focus solely on culture' (pp. 81–82). In-period readers. David Brody (Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9, 1981–82, read): 'During his tenure at Rochester a decade or so ago, Herbert G. Gutman built up a remarkable graduate program in American working-class history … Gregory Kealey's book bears the marks of what might be termed the Gutman school' (p. 361); but 'In one crucial way, unfortunately, it does not': Gutman 'invariably has drawn his ideas out from the evidence', and 'Had he adhered to the prudent craft of his mentor, Kealey might have written a powerful book' (p. 364). Morton (2000, pp. 22–23, read): the 'second generation' 'travelled abroad, to Warwick, Rochester, and Binghamton, to meet their American and British mentors', and the Knights of Labor records 'Kealey had been able to study at Rochester'. Later engagement, title level only: 'Herbert G. Gutman, 1928–1985, and the Writing of Working-Class History' (Monthly Review, 1986) and 'Gutman and Montgomery' (ILWCH, 1990; wcreq_kealey_1990). Gutman and Montgomery are historians on the newleft roster (work_cultures strand). Influence, not discipleship: the 1981 essay also gives Thompson and Williams as touchstones, and edge_890 carries Thompson's place in the field. edge_888 (newleft ↔ cdn_working_class) stays as the group-level comparison.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wallerstein’s world-system grouped with the “Europe-centered stories” whose motor is western Europe’s prior advantages; Pomeranz borrows from them but argues for a late, contingent divergence (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own introduction (2000, pp. 14–16; read by both research passes). Braudel, Wallerstein and Chaudhuri appear with North in "a second group of arguments" that "emphasize the emergence of institutions in early modern Europe" (p. 14); "the motor of Wallerstein’s story is western Europe’s unique combination of relatively free labor, large and productive urban populations, and merchants and governments" (p. 15, as the second pass quotes it); "This work borrows from these arguments—mostly those of the various 'institutionalists'—but ultimately argues for different propositions" (p. 16). A bounded critique of a Eurocentric premise, not a rejection of unequal exchange: he cites Williams, Frank and Amin as earlier arguments from colonial extraction (p. 3 n. 2). The chapter discussions are unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Black Jacobins as a model for analysing “metropole and colony in one lens” (2003)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 533): "Colonizers were made both in the metropole and on colonial sites. And, as C. L. R. James's The Black Jacobins (1938) taught us, much can be gained through the analysis of metropole and colony in one lens." A retrospective acknowledgement made in defending the book's method; it names a resource, not the origin of her project. Her 2014 essay also sets James and Williams against the British Marxist pantheon (History Workshop Journal 78, p. 23, read).

named_group_routes.relationship: Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers in the making of the Industrial Revolution: Inikori's reassertion of Williams (2002), with the 1987 conference volume on Williams's legacy as its precedent
named_group_routes.evidence_note: O'Rourke, EH.Net review of Inikori (2003; read in part): 'His argument is that international trade was crucial to the success of that revolution, in particular trade with the Atlantic Basin (Africa, the West Indies, and the Americas); and that Africans on both sides of the Atlantic were central to this process, both as consumers and producers'; 'a lot of cliometricians will probably conclude that Inikori's argument is not as yet proven'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 227): Inikori is 'Williams' best modern-day defender', concerned that 'the Industrial Revolution owed much more to Africa and Africans than previously thought'. Solow and Engerman (eds, 1987): contents only, with chapters by Solow, Inikori, Richardson and Drescher. Inikori's book itself is unread. Distinct from edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

named_group_routes.relationship: The co-editor of Selected Subaltern Studies (1988) questions Guha’s programme from within: his recovery of subaltern consciousness read as “a strategic use of positivist essentialism” (1985), and his insistence on the “full autonomy” of the subaltern domain not endorsed (1988)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A repair to the pre-2000 core, from existing readings of her own texts. "Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography" (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; read in full for revision 1.137): quoting Elementary Aspects while "Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain" (p. 341), she reads the project of retrieving subaltern consciousness "as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest" (p. 342). "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988; existing reading of the Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha's autonomous domain, "I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy" (p. 79). Collaboration in the same years: Selected Subaltern Studies (Oxford University Press, 1988), edited by Guha and Spivak (title as recorded on said_subaltern_foreword_1988; Roosa, 2006, n. 4, read). A later historian's summary: Eaton (2000, p. 60) reads the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians". edge_984 (Spivak → subaltern, critique) carries her critique of the collective's recovery of consciousness and its neglect of gender, and from this revision no longer names the autonomy claim in its relationship; this edge carries the person-to-person disagreement with Guha's autonomy claim, which Guha's own entry already names among the in-period critiques. A critique from a collaborator, not a rejection.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black Reconstruction (1935) reinterprets emancipation and Reconstruction through Black agency and an interrupted experiment in multiracial democracy, as Chad Williams reads it (2022).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Williams’s introduction, read, supplies this characterization; the full 1935 book is not newly read. The existing field roster is retained, and this contribution does not claim sole founding of Black historical scholarship.

named_group_routes.relationship: Treats historical social science as a challenge to fixed disciplinary boundaries and ahistorical universal laws.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Williams’s framing (p. 203) and Wallerstein’s replies (pp. 206–207), read: historical systems, knowledge structures and disciplinary restructuring. The framing is attributed to Williams. A methodological contribution, without a founding claim or treating future-system predictions as established fact.

named_group_routes.relationship: As Richard J. Ross explains, Rodgers follows Williams’s keyword method while shifting attention toward the political uses and consequences of contested terms.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Ross1998,230,note1,contrasts genealogy with Rodgers’s forensic emphasis and points to Contested Truths(1987),3–16. The note cites Williams’s revised1983 Keywords; its historical edition is not silently changed. Only this substantive introductory note was read in a public reproduced/indexed extract; direct Yale retrieval returned403. Neither complete article nor Rodgers’s and Williams’s books were freshly read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Lears uses Williams’s account of feeling and cultural relations when developing a less mechanical conception of hegemony.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1985invokes structure of feeling and identifies a parallel base/superstructure argument;1973article and The Long Revolution1961pp48–71 are distinct cited works. This is Raymond, not Eric Williams. Complete originals unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians: Indian Affairs records made without consent are read critically and interpreted together with others (2018).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie, community-controlled: cited, not reproduced; its family material is not used). 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018): opening (archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians); section on Library and Archives Canada (records made under the Indian Act without Indigenous knowledge or consent; still vital to Indigenous history); closing paragraph (an interpretive method that involved other people; restricted records under a researcher agreement). verification.note: Review read in full in the Persée text layer, pp. 242–245 (Persée record etchi_0755-5857_1996_num_15_1; OpenAlex W2981359141: vol. 15, issue 1, pp. 242–245). The book is 'ambitieux, intelligent, informé, bien argumenté' but 'ne convainc pas tout à fait'; Huang-Yun, where the Yellow River and Grand Canal cross, covers roughly western Shandong (p. 242). Pomeranz 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', setting Huang's involution model beside the 'breakthrough' theses of Myers, Rawski and Brandt (the OCR reads 'Ramski'); central thesis: the state gave up its priority on reproducing the population and its regional redistribution, concentrating resources on competitive regions and sectors; the 'coût économique, social et écologique' for a region become peripheral 'au sens skinnérien' was extremely heavy; 'La dégradation de l'environnement se taille la part du lion dans la démonstration de K. Pomeranz, qui consacre trois chapitres sur cinq au déboisement du Shandong occidental et au déclin catastrophique des travaux d'entretien du fleuve Jaune et du Grand Canal' (p. 243). Tables and appendices estimate damage from deficient water control to agriculture, transport and trade; a population 'privée de bois' burns straw, grass, roots and animal dung needed as fertiliser; 'Il postule plus qu'il ne prouve une stratégie délibérée de développement sélectif'; praise for 'la remarquable monographie sur le contrôle des eaux du Grand Canal et du fleuve Jaune' (p. 244); chapter 2 on cotton and local social structure (pp. 244–245). sources.citation: Joan Sangster, “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History: Exploring the Past, Present and Future,” Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000): 127ff.

verification.note: Abstract read: thirty years of women’s labour history shaped by feminist, left and labour organizing, international social theory and Canadian historiography; feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history, and calls to integrate race and ethnicity, shifted its narrative and paradigms; gender more effectively though not completely integrated into class formation; post-structuralism and the decline of the left unsettle the field. Checked against: Crossref DOI record; OpenAlex abstract (English and French).
